article.title: Why AI Agents Need a Budget, Not Just Permissions
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Security discussions about AI agents often focus on permissions: which files an agent can read, which APIs it can call, and which actions require human approval. Permissions are essential, but they answer only one question: is an action allowed? They do not answer how much of an allowed resource an agent should be able to consume.

Consider an agent that can search a paid database. Every individual query may be authorized, yet a poorly designed loop could issue thousands of queries and create a large bill. An agent allowed to send internal messages could produce hundreds of unnecessary notifications. A coding agent with access to cloud infrastructure might repeatedly launch tests that consume compute. None of these actions necessarily violates a permission rule.

This suggests a second control layer: budgets. A budget can limit money, API calls, tokens, execution time, database rows, emails, or other scarce resources. The limit can apply to one task, one user, one agent, or a defined period. When the budget is nearly exhausted, the system can slow down, request approval, switch to a cheaper method, or stop.

Budgets are particularly useful because agents can take sequences of actions. Traditional software usually follows a path designed in advance. An agent may choose tools dynamically, observe results, and decide to try again. This flexibility is valuable, but it makes total resource consumption harder to predict from any single action.

A budget should not simply be a hard ceiling. Systems can use warning thresholds and escalation rules. For example, an agent might spend up to $2 automatically, continue to $10 after lightweight approval, and require stronger approval above that level. The control then reflects both autonomy and economic risk.

Time is another useful budget. An agent asked to research a minor question should not necessarily run for two hours because it keeps finding additional sources. A maximum execution time or number of tool calls forces the system to recognize diminishing returns. The agent can return the best result obtained so far and explain what remains uncertain.

Budgets also improve observability. If teams record expected and actual resource use for agent workflows, they can identify inefficient prompts, repeated calls, unusual behavior, or tasks whose economics do not make sense. Cost becomes a design signal rather than merely a monthly surprise.

There is a connection to security as well. Unexpected resource consumption can indicate a malfunction, prompt injection, compromised credential, or runaway loop. Spending and usage limits reduce the blast radius even when the underlying cause has not yet been diagnosed.

Teams should define what happens at the limit before deployment. A budget that simply terminates a critical workflow can create another operational risk. Depending on the task, the right response may be to pause, save state, notify an owner, or request an explicit extension.

Permissions and budgets therefore solve different problems. Permission design asks, ‘May this agent do this?’ Budget design asks, ‘How much may it do before another decision is required?’ A robust agent system needs both. Autonomy without permission boundaries is dangerous, but autonomy without resource boundaries can also be expensive, disruptive, and difficult to govern.
paragraphs.zh: Agent 安全不能只看 permission，還需要 resource budget。每次 API call 都可能合法，但 runaway loop 仍可能造成大量費用或通知。Budget 可以限制金額、token、tool calls、execution time 等，並搭配 warning、approval 與 escalation。它同時改善 cost observability，也能縮小異常或攻擊的 blast radius。
paragraphs.ja: Agentの安全設計ではpermissionだけでなくresource budgetも必要です。個々のAPI callが許可されていても、loopによって大量の費用が発生する可能性があります。金額、token、tool call、execution timeなどへ上限と警告、approvalを設定し、異常時のblast radiusを抑えます。
